## 2. Failure Modes

The choice of failure model determines, almost mechanically, how large a quorum must be and what structural safeguards (durable logs, authentication, Byzantine-tolerant voting) a protocol needs to preserve safety. Weaker (more benign) failure assumptions permit smaller quorums and simpler protocols; stronger (more adversarial) failure assumptions force larger quorums and additional cryptographic or state-machine machinery.

### Crash-Stop (Fail-Stop) Failures

The crash-stop model, also called the fail-stop model, is the most benign failure assumption used in distributed systems theory. A process that fails simply halts and performs no further actions — ever. It does not send corrupted messages, it does not restart, and critically, other processes can often detect that it has crashed (the "stop" in fail-stop implies a reliable or semi-reliable crash-detection mechanism, as in the classical fail-stop model of Schlichting and Schneider, which assumes crash detection is accurate). Because a crashed process contributes nothing — neither correct nor incorrect behavior — to the system going forward, the quorum-sizing requirement under crash-stop failures is the lightest of any model: to tolerate f crash-stop failures among n replicas while guaranteeing that any two quorums intersect in at least one correct (non-crashed) process, it suffices to require quorums of size ⌈(n+1)/2⌉ (a simple majority) with n ≥ 2f+1. This is the textbook majority-quorum requirement: any two majorities out of n ≥ 2f+1 nodes must overlap in at least one node, and since at most f nodes are down at once, that overlap is guaranteed to include at least one live, correct node, which is what makes majority-quorum replication (as used in quorum-based replicated storage) safe under this model.

### Crash-Recovery Failures

The crash-recovery model relaxes crash-stop by allowing a process that has halted to subsequently **restart** and rejoin the protocol. This single change has outsized consequences for protocol design because a recovering process is a liability unless it can reconstruct enough of its prior state to avoid violating safety invariants it had previously promised to uphold — the central danger is commonly called **amnesia**: a process that crashes after having voted for, acknowledged, or committed some value, then restarts with no memory of having done so, and proceeds to cast a vote or take an action inconsistent with its earlier commitment. Amnesia breaks safety properties that depend on a process "remembering" commitments (e.g., not voting for two different values in what it believes are fresh rounds, or not acknowledging a write it has already acknowledged differently). Guarding against amnesia requires **durable (stable) storage**: before a process sends any message that constitutes a promise, vote, or acknowledgment, it must first fsync the relevant state (the promise/vote itself, and any associated term or ballot number) to non-volatile storage, so that on restart it can read back exactly what it had promised before participating further. The quorum-sizing math itself does not change relative to crash-stop — an n ≥ 2f+1 majority quorum still suffices to tolerate f simultaneous crash-recovery failures — but the protocol requirement changes substantially: every durable write to stable storage must occur, and be fsynced, *before* the corresponding message is sent, and the recovery procedure must re-read that durable state and treat it as binding before resuming any role in the protocol. Failing to persist state before acknowledging it, or persisting it but not actually consulting it correctly on restart, reintroduces the possibility of a safety violation even with a nominally sufficient quorum size, because the "node" that comes back is not actually the same reliable participant the quorum arithmetic assumed.

### Byzantine Failures

The Byzantine failure model, named for the Byzantine Generals Problem formalized by Lamport, Shostak, and Pease, is the most severe and general failure assumption: a Byzantine-faulty process may behave in a **completely arbitrary** way, including sending different (and mutually contradictory) messages to different peers, selectively omitting messages, forging or replaying messages, colluding with other faulty processes, or acting with intent to actively subvert the protocol rather than merely failing silently. Byzantine failures subsume every weaker failure model (crash-stop, crash-recovery, omission) as special cases, because arbitrary behavior includes the possibility of simply halting or dropping messages — the Byzantine model is a strict superset of behaviors.

This generality forces both a larger quorum and additional protocol machinery. The standard quorum bound, established originally by Lamport/Shostak/Pease and used in practical BFT protocols like PBFT (Castro and Liskov), is **n ≥ 3f+1** to tolerate f Byzantine faults, in contrast to the n ≥ 2f+1 sufficient for crash-stop/crash-recovery. The reasoning is structural: a quorum must be large enough that any two quorums intersect in at least f+1 nodes, because up to f of the nodes in the intersection could be the same Byzantine nodes lying consistently to both quorums, and the protocol needs at least one surviving *correct* node in every pairwise quorum intersection to prevent two conflicting values from both gathering a quorum of apparent support. With n = 3f+1, a quorum is typically set at 2f+1 nodes; any two such quorums intersect in at least (2f+1)+(2f+1)-(3f+1) = f+1 nodes, which is enough to guarantee at least one honest node in the overlap even if all f Byzantine nodes are placed in that overlap. This is also why Byzantine protocols need more than quorum-size adjustment alone: they additionally require authenticated or at least non-equivocable communication in some form (digital signatures, message authentication codes, or careful use of all-to-all communication/relaying so that equivocation — a Byzantine node telling different peers different things — can be detected or diluted by cross-checking), and typically a multi-phase voting structure (e.g., PBFT's pre-prepare/prepare/commit three-phase protocol) specifically to force Byzantine nodes to either expose inconsistent messages to honest nodes or be unable to prevent honest nodes from reaching agreement.

### Network Partitions (Including Asymmetric Partitions)

A network partition is a failure of the communication substrate, not of the processes themselves: the network splits into two or more subsets of nodes such that messages between subsets are delayed indefinitely or dropped entirely, while nodes within a subset can still communicate normally. From the perspective of a protocol's safety mechanics, a clean (symmetric) partition is often modeled as equivalent to the simultaneous crash of every node on the "other side" from the point of view of any given subset — which is why majority-quorum protocols, designed originally with crash-stop faults in mind, also provide the standard mechanism for surviving partitions: only the subset of nodes containing a majority (more than n/2) can continue to form quorums and make progress, while the minority subset is unable to assemble a quorum and must stall, which is precisely the mechanism that prevents **split-brain** — two disjoint subsets both believing they are authoritative and accepting conflicting writes.

**Asymmetric (or partial) partitions** break this clean equivalence and are considerably more dangerous. In an asymmetric partition, node A may be unable to reach node B, while B can still reach A (e.g., due to a one-directional routing or firewall misconfiguration), or node C may be partitioned from A but not from B, producing a connectivity graph that is not a simple clique split. Protocols that assume partitions are symmetric (i.e., that unreachability is always mutual) can be fooled into inconsistent views of cluster membership: A may consider B dead and proceed without it, while B still considers itself live and able to communicate with a quorum that includes C, producing two concurrently active "majorities" if the asymmetry is exploited incorrectly by a naive failure detector. This does not change the quorum-size formula itself, but it changes the protocol requirement substantially: liveness/failure-detection decisions cannot be made unilaterally from one node's local view of connectivity; a node must only consider itself part of an active quorum if it can positively confirm a full quorum's worth of mutual, bidirectional responsiveness (not merely that it has not heard a "you're excluded" message), and quorum certificates or similar explicit acknowledgment structures are used precisely so that "I have a quorum" is a verifiable, exchanged claim rather than an inferred one from an asymmetric and possibly misleading view of the network.

### Gray Failures

Gray failure describes a category of faults that fall between the clean binary of "up" and "down" assumed by crash-stop models: a node or component is degraded — slow, partially functional, intermittently correct — in a way that is detectable by some observers but not others, and often invisible to the simplistic heartbeat/liveness checks a system relies on for failure detection. A canonical example is a node whose disk I/O has degraded so that it responds to health-check pings (which touch only the network stack) while timing out on actual write operations, or a node experiencing a slow memory leak that causes intermittent, latency-dependent failures rather than a clean crash. The defining property of gray failure, as characterized in systems research (e.g., Huang et al.), is this differential observability: the component is functioning correctly from the perspective of the monitoring/failure-detection subsystem while actually failing from the perspective of the clients or downstream components that depend on its substantive behavior.

Gray failures do not fit neatly into the crash-stop/omission/Byzantine taxonomy because the node is not crashed (it still participates), is not purely silent (it does respond to some things), and is not maliciously arbitrary (its deviations are a byproduct of degradation, not intent) — yet it can violate the implicit assumption nearly every quorum protocol relies on, which is that a "responsive" node is also a "correct and timely" node for the operation actually being performed. The practical consequence for protocol design is that failure detection and quorum formation must be based on health signals specific to the actual critical path (e.g., end-to-end write latency and success, not just liveness pings), and some systems introduce explicit "degraded" or "suspected" states as a third category between up/down so that gray-failing nodes can be excluded from quorums or treated as slow/unreliable (closer to a timing/omission fault, handled by timeouts and retries) even though they have not formally crashed — this does not change the arithmetic minimum quorum size required for safety under crash-stop assumptions, but it does mean that in practice, without gray-failure-aware detection, a quorum can be nominally satisfied (enough nodes "ack") while substantively failing to provide durability or correctness, because one or more of the acking nodes is gray-failed and its acknowledgment does not mean what the protocol assumes it means.
